blocks.text: It is the unclean bird κατ' ἐξοχήν [kat' exochēn], for it is a bird of prey (דורס, see the various explanations of this concept §. 23), it has no crop, has a single-skinned stomach and has no אצבע יתירה (Chulin 61a). The author of the ספר הבריה**) copies the Talmudic statement without further explanation (ibid. Bl. 70, p. 2), although the last part of the statement presents much difficulty. Most take the אצבע יתירה to be the hind toe, which, however, is lacking in none of the species of eagle known to us; they differ only in the number of front toes, thus the golden eagle (Aquila imperialis) has not three but four front toes, yet each of the 10 species of eagle living in Europe has a hind toe; the Tosaphot also remark that the common eagle, איגלא, Aigle, has a hind toe (Tos. Chulin 63a. s.v. נץ); one may therefore probably agree with the explanation of Nissim, who understands by אצבע יתירה the elongation of the front middle toe, which probably need not be the case with some species of eagle. The later decisors (see Peri Megadim on Ture Sahab Jore Dea §. 82, lit. 3), however, decide neither for the one nor for the other explanation***).
The eagle strangles its prey, which it devours at once without waiting for its death (Tos. Chulin 61a. s.v. הדורס).
On the title "Eagle!" cf. §. 107; on its love for its young p. 172, note.
The Osprey.

עוניה (Chulin 62a), and עז (Kelim 17, 14). The wings, which reach to the tip of the tail (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 278), were used for implements (Kelim ibid.). It never stays in places inhabited by humans (בישוב) (Chulin ibid.). Landau translates עז as sea eagle, אוז on the other hand as black eagle (A. Valera); but since the Jerusalem Targum renders עוניה by עוז or אוז, the latter word cannot be the black eagle, since this belongs precisely to the smallest species of eagle, whereas the above-mentioned use of the eagle's wings suggests only a large species of eagle.
The Ossifrage.

פרס, which is mentioned alongside the osprey (§. 194) in Chulin 62a. It too does not stay in inhabited places; the ossifrage belongs to the eagle genus and is the white-tailed sea eagle (Haliaëtos ossifragus), see Voigt l. c. 2. p. 277. It received its name because of its unruliness and ferocity; it stays especially on the seashore and preys on large mammals and birds, such as foxes, bustards, geese etc.
On the eagle species Perknopterus see the Appendix s.v. ירודות.
The Vulture.

After a lengthy discussion the Talmud comes to the conclusion that ראה, דאה, איה and דיה signify one and the same bird, but explains only the word ראה (to see), which indicates the sharp sight of the bird: "It can," it says there, "be in Babylon and nevertheless spot a carcass in Eretz Yisrael."

The gloss considers this statement a metaphor, but concedes the extraordinarily sharp sight of the bird. Now although all birds of prey have a sharp gaze, one can nevertheless see from Rashi (B. mez. 24b) which bird in particular is meant. Here it is related how the bird דיו took a piece of meat from the market and let it fall down into a garden. On this Rashi: עוף שקורין אוולטור והוא לשון דיה "the [p. 168] bird which is called Vulture (vulture), synonymous with ריה."

The sharp eye of the vulture is well known. In the first passage the Talmud adds that in the Orient there are a hundred species of unclean birds, all of which belong to the vulture genus; even if the round number is perhaps not to be taken literally (§. 12), it is nevertheless certain that the vulture genus is very numerous, most of which are found in Africa and Asia. Voigt l. c. 2. p. 282; cf. article Stork (§. 204).
The Griffon Vulture.

This vulture, also called the Contor or Condor, is the largest species of vulture; its outspread wings are said to measure eighteen feet, and its legs are as thick as a man's wrist (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 283). This bird is not mentioned explicitly in the Talmud, but in Rashi (Chulin 25b). The Talmudic passage says that certain implements were made from the claws (צפרנים, §. 54) of a bird; on this Rashi says that this is the גריפין, Griffon, griffon vulture.
The Egyptian Vulture.

Chulin 63a it says: The bird רחם (Lev. 11, 18; in Deut. 14, 17 it reads רחמה) is the שרקרק, but it is called רחם (love) because when it appears love (rain) is granted to the world. The name שרקרק was given to the bird on account of its cry, which sounds Schirkrek.

We leave the many divergent explanations aside (see הכתב והקבלה by J. Meklenburg on Lev. 11, 18), since, as Rosenmüller (loc. cit. p. 317) has demonstrated, the Arabic homophonous رخم [rakham] designates the Egyptian vulture. It is not much larger than our crow, but has long wings; its cry is hissing at first and ends in an unpleasant screeching.
One would accordingly have to imagine that natural sound שרקרק in such a way that the first notes שרק "Tschirk" and the after-sound רק "Reck" are heard as a subsequent screech.
Probably this bird makes its cry heard chiefly at the onset of the hoped-for Nile flood.

It should, however, [p. 169] not go unmentioned that in Arabic the bee-eater (Merops Apiaster) is called شِرِقْراق [shiriqrāq] (Schirikrakon), and here one may indeed choose between the two Arabic names, which correspond to the two names רחם and שרקרק, but which the Talmud assigns to one and the same bird.
In Cuvier this bird (Egyptian vulture) is called Perknopterus, but it is by no means identical with the Περκνόπτερος [Perknopteros] of the ancients, which is dealt with in the Appendix s.v. ירודוח.
The Crane.
Kiduschin 44a it is said: Resch Lakesch cried out like a כרוכיא, on which Rashi: It is the translation of עגור (Jerem. 8, 7) and is called גרואה Grue.
